title: Building the run's host list deep-clones every environment's entire host table once per selected host
existing_state: GetHostConnections (Form1.cs:13301-13392) calls _environmentService.GetActiveEnvironmentVariables() at Form1.cs:13373 INSIDE the per-row loop — once for every selected host. Each call runs ConfigurationService.LoadEnvironmentState (Services/ConfigurationService.cs:174-179), which (a) runs NormalizeEnvironmentData on the cached config (360-403), where EnvironmentConfig.Normalize re-allocates a new Dictionary for every host row of every environment (Models/EnvironmentConfig.cs:83-88); then (b) CloneEnvironmentMap (411-425) deep-clones every environment — every host-row dictionary again (EnvironmentConfig.Clone, 48-69) plus another Normalize pass. Net: ~3 full copies of every host row in every environment, per selected host, just to read the active environment's variables (which cannot change mid-loop). The iterator is materialized with .ToList() on the UI thread at run start (Form1.cs:12277 and 12900) — the SshDebugLog timing instrumentation around it (12276-12278, 'Building host connections') shows this stage was already a latency suspect. For a 500-host run with 3 environments of 500 rows each that is ~1.5 million dictionary copies before the first connection opens. The same clone-everything call also runs on every editor tooltip hover (Form1.cs:709).
recommendation: Hoist the GetActiveEnvironmentVariables() call out of the loop in GetHostConnections — fetch once before the foreach and reuse the dictionary (a one-line move that eliminates the O(selected hosts x environments x env rows) clone storm). Additionally give ConfigurationService a read-only environment accessor that does not clone (or caches the last clone until the next Save invalidates it) so dialog/tooltip read paths stop paying O(all environments x all hosts) allocations per query; LoadEnvironmentState's normalize-on-read mutation of the cached config can move to load/save time where it belongs.
user_benefit: Eliminates a hidden allocation storm at the start of every run — on a 1000-host fleet with a few environments this is millions of dictionary allocations and a multi-second UI freeze before the first connection even opens.
